newsitem.title: USA: Stocks rally after jobs report, blue chips set records.
newsitem.headline: Stocks rally after jobs report, blue chips set records.

text.p: The Dow Jones industrial average jumped more than 130 points to a record high Friday, as bond interest rates tumbled after the May jobs report eased fears of rising interest rates.
The Dow surged 130.49 to close at 7,435.78, beating the old mark of 7,383.41 set on May 27. The increase was the sixth-largest in point terms and gave the Dow a gain of 104.74 points for the week.
The S&P 500 and New York Stock Exchange Composite indexes also set records while the Nasdaq composite index rose 14.79 points to 1,404.84, within 10 points of its record high.
In the broader market, advancing issues outpaces declines by 1,705 to 734 on volume of 488.3 million shares on the NYSE.
Stocks rallied from the opening, barely flinching after the May employment report revealed that the unemployment rate dipped to 4.8 percent in May, the lowest since October 1973.

But the report also indicated slower-than-expected job growth in May, and taken as a whole, analysts said the data showed the economy continues to operate in a nearly ideal fashion for the stock market.
"The report basically said we are in an economy that is performing extremely well without any acceleration of inflation," said Peter Cardillo, director of research at Westfalia Investments.

Bonds, which fell right after the report, changed course and staged a rally of their own, driving the yield on the benchmark 30-year U.S. Treasury down to 6.78 percent, its lowest since Feb. 28, vs. 6.88 percent at Thursday's close. The long bond rose 1-1/8 points, or $12.50 on a $1,000 bond.
Analysts said the bond market's gains were particularly encouraging and, if sustained, could lay the groundwork for an extended stock market rally.

"I think it's pretty clear this is not a one-day wonder," said Peter Canelo, market strategist at Morgan Stanley Dean Witter. "There's a solid case being made in the market that there's no inflation risk," he said. "As long as bonds are settling down, this market is going higher."

Analysts also noted the strong-growth, low-inflation economy was attracting renewed attention from investors abroad, particularly in Europe, where questions mount daily about the political and economic outlook.

"The European monetary union looks like it's having trouble and there is fighting in Germany over their gold policy and uncertainty in France about the polical situation," said Charles Pradilla, market analyst at Cowen & Co.
"Here we are with a strong economy and no sign of inflation troubles so it's not surprising that our assets look attractive."

Financial stocks soared, boosted by the firm bond market. Dow components J.P. Morgan & Co. Inc. rose 2-3/4 to 111-1/2, American Express Co. gained 2-3/8 to 71-3/4 and Travelers Group Inc. climbed 1-3/4 to 57-7/8.
Tech stocks rose as well. Microsoft Corp. climbed 3-1/2 to 124-1/16 and International Business Machines Corp. gained 2-3/4 to 85-5/8.
Drug stocks also rallied, with Pfizer Inc. up 4-1/8 to 107, Eli Lilly & Co. up four to 97-1/8 and Warner-Lambert Co. up four to 102.
First Brands Corp. fell 3-3/8 to 22-5/8 after the company warned that earnings for the fourth quarter and next two quarters would be disappointing.

The Standard & Poor's index of 500 stocks rose 14.58 points to a record 858.01, for a gain of 9.73 on the week. The American Stock Exchange index added 3.90 to 614.65 and was up 9.27 from last Friday.
The NYSE Composite index of all listed common stocks rose 6.49 to 448.13, a record. The average price per share rose 63 cents. The index was up 6.35 on the week.

The Wilshire Associates Equity Index -- the market value of NYSE, American and Nasdaq issues also known as the Wilshire 5000 -- was 8,140.158, up 113.596 or 1.42 percent. The index rose 101.658 for the week.
